title: Workload Profiling and TTFT vs TPOT Acceptance Playbook - Vellum Systems
header:
Date: 2026-12-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Recording: enabled
Location: Zoom
Attendees listed above
Notes: AE+SE-led POC scoping focused on workload profiling, TTFT vs TPOT tradeoffs, p95/p99 targets, sampling and measurement plan, and acceptance criteria.
summary: High-level scoping with Vellum Systems to align POC acceptance criteria: define TTFT (time-to-first-token) and TPOT (total-per-token) SLOs, set p95/p99 latency targets for chat and document-embedding flows, outline sampling strategy and benchmark steps, agree on timeline for pilot deliverables and a live load sweep. Customer emphasized strict p99 for short chat paths (<256 tokens) and concern about tail behavior for long-form summarization. Redwood to provide benchmark harness and suggested traffic replay plan.
topics: TTFT vs TPOT definition and use-cases
p95/p99 target setting for chat and batch jobs
Measurement plan: sampling, synthetic vs replay, KV cache priming
Infrastructure constraints: VPC, encryption, data retention
Timeline and next steps for pilot
transcript:
[00:00:00] Samira Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about an hour, so we want to nail down success criteria for the POC, and specifically the latency SLO conversation TTFT versus TPOT, and the measurement plan.
[00:00:12] Maria Gonzales: Thanks, Samira. High level — we want to know whether Redwood can meet our customer-facing chat p95 at 220ms and p99 at 450ms for short convs. For long-form summarization we're more flexible but worried about tail.
[00:00:28] Jonah Kim: Got it. Quick intro from my side — I'm Jonah, I'm the SE. We'll propose a benchmark harness that runs both single-request (chat) and streaming workloads, and a replay-based run from your production traces.
[00:00:40] Rajesh Iyer: Quick clarification — when you say TTFT you mean from request arrival until first token emitted, right? Not cold-start startup time.
[00:00:47] Lina Duarte: Exactly. TTFT is measured end-to-end from the API ingress to first byte out. TPOT is total-per-token — roughly average per-token latencies across the full generation window; it captures the cost and throughput scaling.
[00:01:00] Tim O'Connell: One of our constraints is a strict p99 for anything under 256 tokens because that's our default interactive mode. Anything above that we batch overnight but we do have an on-demand summarization path.
[00:01:12] Samira Patel: Understood. So possible acceptance thresholds: chat short path p95 220ms, p99 450ms; long-form TTFT p95 800ms, p99 1.6s; TPOT targets for streaming measured as tokens/sec and per-token ms under load. Do those numbers sound reasonable or do we need to adjust?
[00:01:33] Maria Gonzales: p95/p99 numbers sound in the right ballpark. We might push for 400ms p99 on chat if possible but we can start with 450ms.
[00:01:41] Rajesh Iyer: How do you handle prefix caching and KV-cache warmup in benchmarks? Our traffic has a lot of repeated prefixes. If you don't prime caches, TPOT will look worse than reality.
[00:01:52] Jonah Kim: Good question. Our recommended plan has three phases: cold run, warmed run with primed KV-caches using typical prefixes from your traces, and then a sustained load sweep that exercises batching and multi-request concurrency. We'll include cache-priming scripts and a reproducible harness.
[00:02:08] Aisha Noor: And measurement granularity — we want to see p50/p95/p99 and also token throughput per GPU and cost-per-1M-tokens estimates.
[00:02:18] Lina Duarte: We'll capture per-request TTFT and per-token timings. For TPOT we report median token-ms and 95th token-ms across the run, plus aggregate throughput (tokens/s) at different concurrency levels.
[00:02:29] [00:02:30] Maria Gonzales: Are you planning to run in our VPC for the pilot or hosted? We prefer private for data residency.
[00:02:35] Samira Patel: For POC scoping we can do private deployment (VPC) or use Redwood Dedicated — depending on timeline. Private gives you the VPC/KMS controls but adds setup time. We estimated two weeks for a private install; for Dedicated we can start benchmarks faster if that’s acceptable.
[00:02:51] Tim O'Connell: Two weeks for private is fine if the benchmarks are representative. We don't want to bias by network noise.
[00:02:58] Jonah Kim: We'll run the harness inside your VPC so network is consistent with production. Also we'll instrument synthetic traffic and a replay of sampled requests. For replay we need a 24-hour trace with tokens, timestamps, and any routing metadata. Redact PII as needed.
[00:03:14] Rajesh Iyer: We can provide a 24-hour window, but we will only share aggregated request logs, not raw user messages. Is that sufficient?
[00:03:21] Lina Duarte: Aggregated traces with request length, token counts, and prefix fingerprints are sufficient to simulate caching and prefix distribution. For quality regressions we may need a small sample of prompts, but we can do that under an NDA.
[00:03:33] [00:03:35] Maria Gonzales: Let's talk percentiles and sampling. We want the p99 to reflect real traffic tail. What sample size do you use for p99 stability?
[00:03:44] Jonah Kim: We typically run sustained sweeps for 30–60 minutes at each load point to get stable p99 estimates. Statistically, p99 needs thousands of samples; our playbook recommends at least 5k requests per measurement bucket.
[00:03:58] Samira Patel: We also recommend bootstrapped confidence intervals in the reports so you can see margin of error on p99.
[00:04:06] Rajesh Iyer: On the TPOT side, we're concerned about cost. Can you show cost vs latency tradeoffs with quantized model variants?
[00:04:14] Lina Duarte: Yes. Part of the POC is to profile model variants — full FP16 / int8-ish quantization profiles. We'll measure latency, throughput, and unit cost. For some long sequences the per-token cost drops with larger batch sizes, but TTFT can increase if batching introduces extra waiting.
[00:04:31] Tim O'Connell: So we need a clear gating rule: if TTFT degrades beyond X or p99 goes above Y, we'll classify as fail for interactive path.
[00:04:40] Samira Patel: We can propose an acceptance matrix: interactive path (<=256 tokens) must meet p95/p99 thresholds with <5% regressions compared to baseline; long-form path can have lenient TTFT but must meet TPOT cost targets and not exceed p99 thresholds defined.
[00:04:56] Maria Gonzales: Baseline — our current deployment is on in-house GPU fleet using an optimized runtime; we can provide current p95/p99 numbers.
[00:05:03] Jonah Kim: Great, providing a baseline will let us compute delta and show you cost/latency tradeoffs.
[00:05:08] [00:05:10] Aisha Noor: Timeline — what are typical milestones?
[00:05:13] Samira Patel: Proposed timeline: week 0: data & artifact handoff, environment provisioning; week 1: baseline runs + cold/warm passes; week 2: sustained load sweeps and model variant profiling; week 3: final report + recommended config and a 1-week optional soak test. So about 3 weeks active plus optional soak. Private deployment might add 1–2 weeks at the start.
[00:05:36] Rajesh Iyer: Are you able to support our hybrid traffic mix where 70% are short conversational requests, 20% short summarizations, 10% long-form?
[00:05:44] Lina Duarte: Yes, the harness will let us define traffic mix and token-distribution percentiles so we can replay a representative mix. We'll include burstiness and concurrency patterns.
[00:05:54] [00:05:55] Maria Gonzales: One of our compliance folks asked about auditable measurement — we need the harness to produce reproducible artifacts and logs for later audit.
[00:06:03] Jonah Kim: The harness will produce result artifacts, raw timing logs, and a reconciliation report. We can also produce a sanitized CSV that your compliance team can review.
[00:06:11] Tim O'Connell: Any recommendations on sampling strategy for p99 under bursty loads? Our system sees sudden 10x bursts when a few customers run large jobs.
[00:06:20] Samira Patel: We'll run a burst window in the load plan: ramp to normal, then several short 10–20 second bursts at 5–10x to capture tail effects. We'll also include long-tail tail welding — deliberate long-running requests to see eviction behavior.
[00:06:33] [00:06:34] Rajesh Iyer: How do you measure network contribution? If we colocate harness inside the VPC it should be small but still non-zero.
[00:06:40] Jonah Kim: We'll instrument from client-side (inside VPC) and server-side to split network vs runtime timings. We'll present a breakdown: ingress latency, runtime TTFT, tokenization overhead, and egress. If network variance is >5% of p95, we'll surface that.
[00:06:55] Samira Patel: On instrumentation: we can add tracing hooks to your request path, or you can provide logs with timestamps. We prefer distributed traces but logs are OK.
[00:07:05] [00:07:10] Maria Gonzales: Clarify the measurement of TPOT. Is that per-token average ms across all tokens, or per-request total divided by token count?
[00:07:18] Lina Duarte: We'll compute both: per-token latency (ms/token at token index distribution) and normalized per-request tokens. TPOT as we use it is the end-to-end per-token cost including batching overheads — so it reflects how many tokens/sec you get at a given concurrency.
[00:07:33] Rajesh Iyer: We also want to watch out for KV cache blowups for longer contexts. If you have a 10k token history, memory and KV cache eviction change latency characteristics.
[00:07:43] Jonah Kim: We'll include a context-length sweep: 64/256/1024/2048/5k/10k depending on model limit. If your app uses sliding windows frequently we can simulate eviction cycles.
[00:07:55] [00:07:56] Aisha Noor: For reporting, we need a single-sheet acceptance matrix that our legal and procurement people can sign off on.
[00:08:03] Samira Patel: We'll produce that: acceptance matrix with numeric gates (TTFT p95/p99, TPOT throughput, cost thresholds), a sampling plan, and runbook notes.
[00:08:12] Maria Gonzales: About fallback behavior — if p99 spikes in production, we need automatic fallback to a smaller model. Is that part of the POC?
[00:08:19] Lina Duarte: We can demonstrate a model-variant fallback policy in Dedicated or Private. The POC can include an A/B or canary that switches to a lower-latency variant on breach, and we'll simulate failover during the load sweep.
[00:08:31] Rajesh Iyer: Good. For the metrics, besides p95/p99 we want SLO burn rate charts and alert thresholds in the dashboard.
[00:08:39] Jonah Kim: We'll include SLO burn visualization and alert thresholds. Console will provide trace links back to request IDs.
[00:08:47] [00:08:50] Samira Patel: Ok let's capture explicit acceptance criteria — I'll read proposed gating and we can adjust:
[00:08:55] Samira Patel: Interactive chat path (<=256 tokens): TTFT p95 <= 220ms; TTFT p99 <= 450ms; TPOT median token-ms within 15% of baseline; no more than 3% of requests with errors; pass warm-run with primed caches.
[00:09:12] Maria Gonzales: Agree to start. We'll try to reduce p99 later, but for POC those gates are okay.
[00:09:17] Samira Patel: Long-form summarization (>=512 tokens): TTFT p95 <= 800ms; TTFT p99 <= 1.6s; TPOT tokens/sec >= X (we'll compute in report) and cost per 1k tokens must be within committed budget.
[00:09:30] Rajesh Iyer: We need the POC to show cost crosswalks so we can justify any migration.
[00:09:35] Lina Duarte: We'll include cost estimates at different traffic volumes, and show break-even by month given your traffic profile.
[00:09:42] [00:09:45] Aisha Noor: Who owns the runbook and how do we share artifacts?
[00:09:49] Samira Patel: Redwood will own benchmark harness and produce artifact repo; we will give you a link to results and a deck. We'll also hand over scripts so you can re-run locally.
[00:09:58] Maria Gonzales: On SLAs — for Dedicated we expect a latency SLA outline; will that be part of contracting?
[00:10:05] Samira Patel: Yes, SLA language and availability targets are in the Dedicated contract. We'll surface suggested latency SLOs in the POC report but contractual SLAs are part of later procurement.
[00:10:13] [00:10:15] Jonah Kim: Technical note — we'll compare model variants including quantized builds; you'll see tradeoffs where int8 reduces cost ~30% but can add noise in longer sequences. We recommend sanity checks on n-gram overlap for longer outputs for quality signal.
[00:10:30] Rajesh Iyer: We'll add a small eval set for quality checks.
[00:10:34] Lina Duarte: Perfect. About the measurement schedule: we recommend three benchmark runs per day across a week for different timezones and load profiles, but for the POC we can do two representative days.
[00:10:44] [00:10:45] Tim O'Connell: Ok timeline acceptance — sounds good. 
[00:10:48] Maria Gonzales: Let's talk deliverables and owners — what do we expect by next week?
[00:10:52] Samira Patel: Action items coming up: we'll draft benchmark plan and acceptance matrix, provide install checklist for private deployment, request 24-hour aggregated trace by EOD Monday, and schedule an environment provisioning call.
[00:11:05] Rajesh Iyer: We'll need an NDA for any sample prompts. Procurement handles that.
[00:11:10] Samira Patel: We'll send a standard short NDA; we can also accept a redlined version.
[00:11:14] [00:11:20] Aisha Noor: Any open questions from our side?
[00:11:22] Tim O'Connell: One more — how do you capture QoS degradation due to multi-tenant interference on Dedicated?
[00:11:29] Jonah Kim: On Dedicated we provide isolation via GPU pools; we'll also run contention tests and surface worst-case p99. For Private, it's a single-tenant install so interference is low.
[00:11:40] [00:11:41] Maria Gonzales: Ok that covers the highlights. I want a written acceptance matrix to present to procurement.
[00:11:46] Samira Patel: We'll send that by Thursday. Any other items?
[00:11:50] Rajesh Iyer: Please include the exact measurement command lines so our infra can prepare.
[00:11:56] Lina Duarte: We'll include reproducible scripts and a sample terraform/ansible snippet for provisioning.
[00:12:03] Samira Patel: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with notes and next steps.
[00:12:07] Maria Gonzales: Thanks, talk soon.
